summary: Defines the Encapsulating Security Payload, a header that can provide confidentiality, data origin authentication and replay protection for IPv4 and IPv6 packets. It is the part of IPsec that actually encrypts traffic. It was replaced by RFC 4303 and RFC 4305.

plainLanguage.summary: ESP is like putting your letter in an opaque envelope and sealing it. Anyone along the way can see the envelope travel past but cannot read what is inside.

questions: what is the encapsulating security payload
what is the esp header format
what is the difference between transport and tunnel mode
subtitle: The original IPsec header that encrypts and authenticates IP packets, replaced by RFC 4303.

tldr.problem: IP packets cross the network in the clear, so anyone along the path can read them, change them or replay them.
tldr.mechanism: ESP wraps the protected data in a header and trailer that can provide confidentiality, data origin authentication, connectionless integrity and replay protection, in transport mode or tunnel mode.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2406 has been obsoleted by RFC 4303 and RFC 4305, which now define ESP and its algorithm requirements.

today: RFC 2406 was obsoleted by RFC 4303 and RFC 4305, so those are the current ESP specifications. It had itself obsoleted RFC 1827.

sections.title: What ESP Provides
sections.content:
The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) header is designed to provide a mix of security services in IPv4 and IPv6. It can be used alone, together with the IP Authentication Header (AH), or nested through tunnel mode. It works between two hosts, between two security gateways, or between a gateway and a host.

ESP can provide confidentiality, data origin authentication, connectionless integrity, an anti-replay service and limited traffic flow confidentiality. Which of these you get depends on options chosen when the Security Association (SA) is set up. Confidentiality and authentication are each optional, but at least one of them MUST be selected.

The text warns that confidentiality without integrity or authentication may expose traffic to active attacks that undermine the confidentiality. The anti-replay service can only be selected when authentication is selected, and it is up to the receiver to turn it on.
sections.plainLanguage: ESP is a toolbox for keeping network messages private and untampered. You pick which tools you want, but you must pick at least one.

sections.title: The ESP Packet Format
sections.content:
The IP header just before ESP carries the value 50 in its Protocol (IPv4) or Next Header (IPv6) field. The ESP packet then holds, in order: a Security Parameters Index (SPI), a Sequence Number, the Payload Data, optional Padding, a Pad Length, a Next Header field and optional Authentication Data.

The SPI is an arbitrary 32-bit value that, with the destination address and the ESP protocol, identifies the SA. Values 1 through 255 are reserved by IANA, and zero is for local use and MUST NOT be sent on the wire. The Sequence Number is an unsigned 32-bit counter that is always sent. The first packet on an SA carries 1, and with anti-replay enabled the counter must never cycle, so a new SA is needed before the 2^32nd packet.

Padding may be 0 to 255 bytes. It fills out block ciphers, keeps the Authentication Data on a 4-byte boundary, and may also hide the true payload length. If the algorithm does not define padding, the default is the byte sequence 1, 2, 3, and so on, which the receiver SHOULD check. Pad Length says how many pad bytes precede it. Next Header is an 8-bit field naming the type of data in the payload. The Authentication Data holds an Integrity Check Value (ICV) computed over the ESP packet minus the Authentication Data.
sections.plainLanguage: An ESP packet is a sealed parcel with a label saying which secret code was used, a count of how many parcels have been sent, the hidden contents, and a tamper-proof seal at the end.

sections.title: Transport Mode and Tunnel Mode
sections.content:
In transport mode ESP is inserted after the IP header and before the upper layer protocol such as TCP or UDP. It protects the upper layer data but not the IP header, and the RFC says it applies only to host implementations. In IPv6 ESP is treated as an end-to-end payload, so it appears after hop-by-hop, routing and fragmentation extension headers.

In tunnel mode the inner IP header carries the ultimate source and destination, while an outer IP header may carry other addresses, such as those of security gateways. ESP protects the entire inner IP packet, including its header. When ESP is implemented in a security gateway to protect transit traffic, tunnel mode must be used, and traffic flow confidentiality needs tunnel mode as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Transport mode seals just the letter inside and leaves the address on the outside as it was. Tunnel mode puts the whole letter, address and all, inside a new envelope with a new address.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving ESP Packets
sections.content:
To send, the implementation finds the SA, puts the payload into the ESP Payload field (just the upper layer data in transport mode, the whole original datagram in tunnel mode), adds padding, then encrypts the payload, padding, Pad Length and Next Header. If authentication is selected, encryption is done first and the ICV is computed over the result. This order lets a receiver reject replayed or bogus packets before decrypting, and allows decryption to run in parallel with authentication.

The sender's counter starts at 0 when the SA is set up. If anti-replay is enabled (the default), the sender MUST NOT send a packet that would make the Sequence Number cycle. Fragmentation, if needed, happens after ESP processing.

On receipt, any reassembly happens first, and a packet that still looks like a fragment MUST be discarded. The receiver looks up the SA from the destination address, the ESP protocol and the SPI, and discards the packet if there is no valid SA. Anti-replay uses a sliding receive window. A minimum window size of 32 MUST be supported, and 64 is preferred as the default. The window is only updated after the ICV check succeeds. The receiver then verifies the ICV, decrypts, and processes the padding.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender locks the message first and then stamps it. The receiver checks the stamp and the ticket number before opening anything, so fake or repeated messages get thrown out early.

sections.title: Algorithms, Auditing and Conformance
sections.content:
A compliant ESP implementation MUST support these mandatory-to-implement algorithms: DES in CBC mode, HMAC with MD5, HMAC with SHA-1, the NULL authentication algorithm and the NULL encryption algorithm. The NULL algorithms exist because encryption and authentication are each optional, but they MUST NOT both be NULL. The RFC adds that a compliant implementation SHOULD NOT offer anti-replay on manually keyed SAs.

Auditing is only required if the system supports it. Then ESP MUST support auditing and let an administrator turn it on or off. Events such as discarded fragments, missing SAs and failed ICV checks are auditable, with a suggested minimum of log data (for example the SPI, time received, addresses and Sequence Number). The receiver is not required to send any message back to the purported sender, because of the risk of inducing denial of service.

The Security Considerations section is short: security is central to the protocol, so it permeates the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone has to know the same few secret-code methods so their devices can understand each other. Writing down suspicious events in a logbook is allowed, but you should not shout back at the sender.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 1827
sections.content:
This document replaced RFC 1827. The major difference is that RFC 2406 specifies a complete framework and context for ESP, whereas RFC 1827 provided a shell that was completed by separate transform documents. The growing number of transforms motivated the rewrite.

Fields once defined in transform documents are now part of the base specification, including the fields for authentication and anti-replay, for padding, and for next protocol identification. The matching packet processing rules are included too.
sections.plainLanguage: The first version was an empty form that every add-on document had to fill in. This version includes all the boxes in one place.
